- **Keyboard-first UI.** The [search screen](https://docs.hypertask.ai/features/search-screen/) is a keyboard-first way to find tasks, and the app publishes its [keyboard shortcuts](https://docs.hypertask.ai/features/keyboard-shortcuts/).
- **AI agents.** Agents [pick up board work](https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/workflows/) over MCP and the CLI.
- **BYOK plan.** [Bring Your Own Key](https://docs.hypertask.ai/features/byok/) uses your own model keys. [Included AI](https://docs.hypertask.ai/features/ai-features/#included-ai-allowance) describes the Free, Pro, and BYOK allowances.","excerpt":"Switching from Trello, Jira, Asana, or Linear. Hypertask has no task import. Create tasks with an agent over MCP or the CLI.","category":"Getting Started","created_at":1794036466,"updated_at":1794840586,"url":"https://docs.hypertask.ai/getting-started/switching/"}

{"id":"docs-getting-started-troubleshooting-login","title":"Troubleshooting Login","slug":"docs-getting-started-troubleshooting-login","content":"## Getting stuck at the login page

If the page appears stuck or doesn't finish loading, check these conditions:

- **Browser cookies are blocked**: Clear cookies or open the site in an incognito window to test if the issue resolves
- **Popup blockers are enabled**: Allow popups for `hypertask.ai` to ensure authentication flows complete
- **Network proxy or VPN**: Temporarily disable your proxy and try again

Some privacy-focused browser extensions and add-ons lock built-in Error objects to protect you from JavaScript errors. In rare cases this blocks Hypertask from properly creating error messages.

To work around this, try one of the following:

- Disable privacy extensions during login, then re-enable them once you've signed in
- Open Hypertask in an Incognito window with extensions disabled — this is the quickest way to verify the issue is related to an extension

## "Email not found" or "Invalid email"

Create a free account or contact your team administrator if you don't see an option to sign up.

## Resetting password

1. Click **Log in**
2. Select **Forgot password**
3. Enter your email address and follow the password-reset link sent to your inbox
4. If you don't receive a reset email, check your spam folder or [get help](https://docs.hypertask.ai/getting-started/contact-support/)

## Account switching behavior

When you start a new login for a different account from the same browser:

- All authentication cookies are properly invalidated after a sign-out (Max-Age=0)
- New session cookies are set for the new account
- Both Better Auth and user identity cookies are refreshed correctly
- You're immediately redirected to a board as the new user

Your logged-in state persists across sessions; hiding or closing the browser doesn't automatically log you out unless you explicitly sign out. Authentication is verified server-side on each request via the signed `ht_session` cookie.

## Sign-in security improvements (hypertask.ai login)

- The sign-in email endpoint no longer returns verification codes or magic-link tokens to callers. This prevents callers from using the response to reset or take over an email account without direct access to the inbox.
<iframe style="width: 100%; height: 100%;" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/J7GYxffM7FE" title="Hypertask Live Demo" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen></iframe>

- Legacy API routes requiring only a non-authenticated session are now protected with signed login checks. Logged-out requests are now refused on all legacy routes, and the system uses verified `ht_session` cookies for all route access.
- A valid sign-out invalidates login cookies in the browser and refreshes Better Auth sessions on the server, preventing copied or reused cookies from granting continued access after a user signs out.
<iframe style="width: 100%; height: 100%;" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/T4JnbqyPovw" title="Hypertask Quickstart" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen></iframe>

Your credentials and login processes otherwise remain unchanged; simply use your email and password or the password reset flow as usual. If you receive password reset emails or confirmations, verify they were sent by `hypertask.ai`; invalid or forwarded reset links are not sent by Hypertask.

---

If none of these steps resolve your issue, [get help](https://docs.hypertask.ai/getting-started/contact-support/).","excerpt":"Common issues and solutions for signing in, resetting passwords, and resolving authentication errors in Hypertask.","category":"Getting Started","created_at":1792923267,"updated_at":1794840591,"url":"https://docs.hypertask.ai/getting-started/troubleshooting-login/"}

{"id":"docs-mcp-agent-webhooks","title":"Agent webhooks","slug":"docs-mcp-agent-webhooks","content":"A webhook is a signed HTTPS request Hypertask sends to a URL you control. Use a team webhook when you want events from your team and you do not want to set up an agent. Use an agent webhook when you want an agent to wake up. Polling still works without a webhook, but the agent learns about changes on its next check instead of immediately. ## Team webhooks, no agent needed You do not need an agent to get a webhook when a task changes in your team. Open **Settings** (gear icon), then **Connect**, then **Webhooks**. The **How webhooks work** link on that page opens this article. Hypertask sends a signed request to your own URL the moment something happens in this team. No agent needed. Each endpoint has its own secret and delivery log. Only the team owner can add or manage these endpoints. A team can have up to 20 endpoints. 1. Under **Add endpoint**, enter a public HTTPS URL. Hypertask POSTs JSON there and signs every request. The URL cannot be `localhost` or a private network address. 2. Under **Board scope**, leave **All boards in this team**, or choose one board. 3. Leave the events you want selected, then select **Add endpoint**. 4. Copy the signing secret now. Hypertask shows it once. It starts with `whsec_`. Use it to verify the `X-Hypertask-Signature` header. See [Verify the signature](#verify-the-signature). 5. Leave **Enabled** on, then select **Send test**. Your URL receives a signed `ping` delivery. Confirm it in that endpoint's delivery log. Store the signing secret in your secret manager. **Rotate secret** replaces it and shows the new value once. **Delete** removes the endpoint. | Event | When Hypertask sends it | |---|---| | `task.created` | A task is created | | `task.updated` | A task's section, status, or due date changes | | `task.assigned` | A person or agent is assigned to a task | | `task.unassigned` | A person or agent is removed from a task | | `comment.created` | A comment is added to a task | | `comment.mention` | A comment mentions one or more agents | Each request is JSON with `id`, `event`, `deliveredAt`, and `data`. Task events put the task under `data.task` (`id`, `ticketNumber`, `projectId`, `title`) and the actor under `data.actor` (`userId`, `agentId`). `task.updated` also includes `data.changes` with at least one of `section`, `status`, or `dueDate`. A test payload uses `event: "ping"` and has no task. ```json { "id": "53d179e1-84b8-48a3-807a-cf8e5b88930b", "event": "task.updated", "deliveredAt": "2026-08-13T10:15:00.000Z", "data": { "task": { "id": 27397, "ticketNumber": "DOC-12", "projectId": 15, "title": "Ship the release notes" }, "changes": { "status": { "from": "Normal", "to": "Archive" } }, "actor": { "userId": 6, "agentId": null } } } ``` On an endpoint you can turn **Enabled** off, **Send test**, **Rotate secret**, or **Delete**. Hypertask refuses **Send test** and **Retry** while the endpoint is disabled. On a delivery, **Retry** queues that event again with a fresh delivery ID. Automatic retries back off across 6 attempts over about 48 minutes. Return any 2xx response within 5 seconds. ## Get your first verified delivery 1. In Hypertask, press **Ctrl+K**, open **Manage agents**, then select the plug icon beside your agent. 2. Under **Wake this agent without polling**, enter your public HTTPS receiver. Optionally limit delivery to one board or a subset of events. 3. Select **Save webhook** and store the signing secret. Hypertask shows it once. 4. Select **Send test**. Your receiver gets a real signed `webhook.test` delivery through the same queue and retry path as production events. 5. Confirm a 2xx result under **Recent deliveries**. Failed deliveries show their status and can be replayed. Store the `whsec_…` signing secret in your secret manager. Hypertask masks it after creation. Rotate it if it is lost or exposed. ## Subscribe from an agent An agent bearer token manages its own endpoint with `self`. A human account token can replace `self` with an owned agent UUID. ### CLI ```bash # Configure all addressed events hypertask webhook configure \ --url https://agent.example.com/hypertask \ --event comment.mention \ --event task.assigned \ --event task.unassigned \ --event comment.created \ --event task.updated \ --event task.created # Prove the receiver, signature, queue, and response path hypertask webhook test # Inspect delivery status hypertask webhook get ``` Use `--agent AGENT_UUID` when running with a human account token. Other commands are `replay DELIVERY_ID`, `rotate-secret`, and `delete`. ### MCP Call `hypertask_webhooks` (`action: "configure"`): ```json { "action": "configure", "input": { "agent_id": "self", "url": "https://agent.example.com/hypertask", "events": ["comment.mention", "task.assigned", "task.unassigned", "comment.created", "task.updated", "task.created"] } } ``` Actions are `get`, `configure`, `test`, `replay`, `rotate`, and `delete`. `replay` also requires `delivery_id`. ### AI Chat / HyperAI In private AI Chat, ask in plain language: > Configure the webhook for my Release Agent at https://agent.example.com/hypertask, then send a test. Secret-bearing and write actions require confirmation before they run. Hypertask shows a preview first; approve it in your next message. In a HyperAI ticket comment, `get`, `test`, `replay`, and `delete` are available with the same confirmation policy. Configure or rotate in private AI Chat, CLI, MCP, or agent settings because HyperAI never writes signing secrets into persistent ticket comments. ### HTTP API ```bash curl -X POST https://app.hypertask.ai/api/mcp/webhooks \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $AGENT_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "action": "configure", "agent_id": "self", "url": "https://agent.example.com/hypertask", "events": ["comment.mention", "task.assigned", "task.unassigned", "comment.created", "task.updated", "task.created"] }' ``` The response contains `secret` once. Read configuration and recent attempts with: ```bash curl "https://app.hypertask.ai/api/mcp/webhooks?agent_id=self" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $AGENT_TOKEN" ``` ## Board-level webhooks Each managed agent has one webhook subscription. Leave **Board scope** empty to receive selected events from every board the agent belongs to, or choose one board to narrow delivery. Hypertask stops delivery if the agent loses that board membership or is revoked. Only the agent owner can view, configure, test, replay, rotate, or delete its webhook. Agent credentials may manage their own webhook with `agent_id: "self"`; a human credential must name an agent it owns. ## Verify the signature Hypertask signs the exact raw request bytes. Verify them before parsing JSON; parsing and reserializing can change the signed content. | Header | Meaning | |---|---| | `X-Hypertask-Event` | Event name, including `webhook.test` | | `X-Hypertask-Timestamp` | Unix time used in the signature | | `X-Hypertask-Delivery` | Stable ID used to deduplicate automatic retries | | `X-Hypertask-Signature` | `sha256=` followed by the lowercase HMAC hex digest | ```text signed content = X-Hypertask-Timestamp + "." + raw request bytes signature = "sha256=" + HMAC-SHA256(signing secret, signed content) ``` Use a constant-time comparison and reject timestamps outside your replay window. The examples use five minutes. ### Node.js / Express ```js import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto"; import express from "express"; const app = express(); const secret = process.env.HYPERTASK_WEBHOOK_SECRET; app.post("/hypertask", express.raw({ type: "application/json" }), (req, res) => { const rawBody = req.body; const timestamp = req.header("x-hypertask-timestamp") ?? ""; const received = req.header("x-hypertask-signature") ?? ""; const timestampSeconds = Number(timestamp); if (!secret || !Buffer.isBuffer(rawBody) || !Number.isFinite(timestampSeconds) || Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - timestampSeconds) > 300) { return res.sendStatus(401); } const digest = createHmac("sha256", secret) .update(`${timestamp}.`) .update(rawBody) .digest("hex"); const expected = `sha256=${digest}`; const left = Buffer.from(received, "utf8"); const right = Buffer.from(expected, "utf8"); if (left.length !== right.length || !timingSafeEqual(left, right)) { return res.sendStatus(401); } const deliveryId = req.header("x-hypertask-delivery"); const payload = JSON.parse(rawBody.toString("utf8")); res.sendStatus(202); // Store deliveryId before queueing work so retries do not run twice. }); ``` ### Python / Flask ```python import hashlib import hmac import json import os import time from flask import Flask, request app = Flask(__name__) secret = os.environ["HYPERTASK_WEBHOOK_SECRET"].encode() @app.post("/hypertask") def handle_webhook(): raw_body = request.get_data(cache=True) timestamp = request.headers.get("X-Hypertask-Timestamp", "") received = request.headers.get("X-Hypertask-Signature", "") try: if abs(time.time() - int(timestamp)) > 300: return "stale timestamp", 401 except ValueError: return "invalid timestamp", 401 signed = timestamp.encode() + b"." + raw_body expected = "sha256=" + hmac.new(secret, signed, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest() if not hmac.compare_digest(received, expected): return "invalid signature", 401 delivery_id = request.headers.get("X-Hypertask-Delivery") payload = json.loads(raw_body) # queueAgentWork(delivery_id, payload) return "", 202 ``` ## Events and payloads | Event | When it fires | Event-only fields | |---|---|---| | `comment.mention` | A comment mentions this exact agent | `commentId`, `commentHtml` | | `task.assigned` | This agent becomes a task assignee | Common task fields only | | `task.unassigned` | This agent is removed from a task | Common task fields only | | `comment.created` | Any comment is added to a task assigned to this agent | `commentId`, `commentHtml` | | `task.updated` | A task in scope changes section, status, or labels | `changes`, optional `labelsRedacted` | | `task.created` | Task creation and automatic column assignment finish in scope | `assignees`, `labels`, optional `labelsRedacted` | | `webhook.test` | The owner selects **Send test** or requests a test | `test: true`, `message`; no task fields | Task event payloads include `event`, `deliveryId`, `occurredAt`, `agentId`, `projectId`, `taskId`, nullable `ticketNumber`, `taskTitle`, and `actor`. Event-only fields appear as shown above. A test payload has the common delivery fields but no task or actor. ```json { "event": "comment.mention", "deliveryId": "53d179e1-84b8-48a3-807a-cf8e5b88930b", "occurredAt": "2026-08-13T10:15:00.000Z", "agentId": "f95165ad-36b3-4d87-af70-547df78e17c1", "projectId": 15, "taskId": 27397, "taskTitle": "Outbound webhooks for agent mentions and assignments", "commentId": 182293, "commentHtml": "

@Release Agent please review

", "actor": { "userId": 6, "agentId": null, "displayName": "Valentin Yeo" } } ``` ## Test and replay **Send test** creates a real `webhook.test` delivery for the active subscription. It uses the same signed request, queue, retry schedule, and recent-delivery list as production events, without requiring a task change. **Replay** is available only to the agent owner and only for a delivery from that agent's current subscription. It copies the stored event payload into a new delivery with a new delivery ID, transport timestamp, and signature. The receiver must treat replay as a possible duplicate of the original work. ## Delivery behavior - Hypertask sends the first `POST` immediately with `Content-Type: application/json`. - Return any 2xx response within **5 seconds**. Queue longer work after responding. - A failed `chat.message` attempt remains available to agent polling while its normal webhook retries continue. If polling claims the message first, Hypertask cancels the outstanding webhook retry so the agent cannot process it twice. Deleting the webhook also releases chat messages that have not been acknowledged. - Events retry after a timeout, network failure, unsafe address, redirect, or any other non-2xx response. Delays after the first, second, and third failed attempts are approximately **30 seconds, 5 minutes, and 30 minutes**. Delivery stops after four total attempts. - Automatic retries keep the exact body and delivery ID. Each attempt gets a fresh timestamp and signature. Store `X-Hypertask-Delivery` before starting work so a retry cannot run the same action twice. - Recent delivered, failed, and cancelled outcomes remain visible for 30 days. ## No public HTTPS URL A webhook cannot point to `localhost` or a private network address. You can expose only your receiver through a temporary tunnel, or skip the webhook and poll. ### Use a temporary Cloudflare Tunnel 1. Start your receiver locally, for example at `http://localhost:3000/hypertask`. 2. Run `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000`. 3. Copy the generated `https://…trycloudflare.com` address, add `/hypertask`, and save it as the webhook endpoint. 4. Select **Send test**, then confirm a 2xx result under **Recent deliveries**. Expose only the webhook route. Do not run a debug server or expose admin routes. Keep the signing secret in an environment variable, do not print secrets or full production payloads, and stop the tunnel when testing ends. Quick Tunnel addresses change when restarted, so update the saved endpoint before testing again. ### Poll instead A webhook is optional. `hypertask agent poll` reads unseen comments that mention the active agent. A persistent worker can also reconcile assignments and its configured board queue through normal authenticated reads, which catches a missed webhook. ```bash hypertask agent poll \ --project "$PROJECT_ID" \ --agent-id "$AGENT_ID" \ --agent-name "$AGENT_NAME" ``` Polling cadence belongs to the worker deployment, not the Hypertask API. Set an explicit active and idle interval in the worker profile. For example, `pollFastSeconds: 60` checks every minute while work is active and `pollSlowSeconds: 3600` checks hourly while idle. A webhook remains the instant path; reconciliation is the slower safety net. ## Troubleshooting | Symptom | Check | |---|---| | No secret appears | Secrets are shown only after first configuration or rotation. Rotate if the original was not stored. | | Test stays pending | Confirm the endpoint is public HTTPS and wait for queue delivery. If it is local, start the tunnel and save its current address. | | `401` from your receiver | Verify the raw bytes before parsing and include `timestamp + "."` before the body. | | Repeated work | Deduplicate with `X-Hypertask-Delivery`; automatic retries are intentionally at least once. | | `4xx` while configuring | The agent must belong to the selected board, and the URL cannot resolve to a private or reserved address. | | No production events | Confirm **Delivery enabled**, selected event names, board scope, and current agent board membership. |","excerpt":"Get a signed webhook when a task changes in your team, with no agent, or wake an agent. Covers verification and working without a public URL.","category":"Agents","created_at":1792923269,"updated_at":1794840600,"url":"https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/agent-webhooks/"}

{"id":"docs-mcp-agents","title":"Creating Agents","slug":"docs-mcp-agents","content":"This guide covers the complete agent onboarding flow in Hypertask — from creating your first agent to adding it to your Kanban board where it can be assigned tasks, mentioned in comments, and controlled via MCP clients or agentic CLIs. ## Overview Agents in Hypertask act as autonomous team members. They have their own identity, can be assigned tasks, receive notifications, and interact with the board using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) or the Hypertask CLI. ## Creating an agent See [Connect a new agent](https://docs.hypertask.ai/connect-an-agent/) for the complete setup. 1. **Create an agent.** Choose one path: - **Agent Chat:** Open [Agent Chat](https://app.hypertask.ai/agents/chat), choose **+ Add agent**, enter a name, and choose **Create**. The agent starts with no boards. Copy the token shown once before choosing **Done**. - **From a board:** Open a team board and use **Ctrl+K > Create agent**. Enter a name, keep **External** selected for your own runtime, and choose **Create**. This attaches the agent to that board and opens its page. If you did not copy a token, use **Access key > Regenerate** there and copy the new token. 2. **Add boards.** The person who owns the agent opens [Agents](https://app.hypertask.ai/agents), opens the agent, expands **Board access**, and ticks each board they want it to use. Changes save immediately. Turn the agent on first if disabled. **Board settings > Agents** only lists agents already attached to that board. It has no add control. Private agents are visible only to their owner. An agent can only join boards in its team; the first board establishes that team. An agent cannot add itself to a board, whatever its role. Admin agents can add other agents of the same owner only on boards they already belong to. Promoting an agent to admin is not an onboarding fix; its owner must grant access first. ## Managing agents Open [Agents](https://app.hypertask.ai/agents) and select your agent to manage its **Board access** and **Access key**. Use **Regenerate** to replace a lost token or **Revoke** to remove it. ### Monitoring agent work Open an agent from the Agents page to see what its worker is doing now. The detail page shows: - **Working now:** The active ticket, elapsed time, runtime, model, heartbeat, and latest progress. - **Queue:** Source-column, worker-queue, assigned, unowned, specialist-owned, and direct-mention counts. - **Up next:** The worker's actual ticket order. Desktop shows the next three tickets; mobile shows the next two. - **Runtime health:** Whether the worker is Working, Connected, Waiting, Stalled, or Offline. - **Recent actions:** The agent's latest comments, evidence, questions, sessions, and model usage. Live worker data is labeled **Live worker**. If no current runtime snapshot exists, Hypertask can show assigned work as **Inferred from board** so it is not mistaken for a live queue. The enabled switch and runtime health answer different questions. An agent can be enabled while its worker is offline. A worker becomes stalled after three missed progress intervals, with a minimum threshold of five minutes. ## Connecting an agent Hypertask agents support two connection methods: **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** for direct client integration, and the **Hypertask CLI** for terminal-based and scripted workflows. Both methods use a bearer token issued per agent. The access key is for a managed agent's own identity, and connecting your own editor (VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code) uses your personal API key from **Settings** (gear icon) → **Connect** → **MCP** instead ([Authentication](https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/overview/#authentication)). ### Retrieving the agent token 1. Open [Agents](https://app.hypertask.ai/agents) and open the agent you own. 2. Find **Access key**. If you no longer have the token, choose **Regenerate**. 3. Copy the new token and store it securely. Use it in the connection examples below. Regenerating a token invalidates the previous one. Tokens have no expiry but can be revoked or replaced. ### Connection methods ### MCP Client Paste the entire configuration snippet into your AI tool (e.g., Claude Desktop, Cursor, or Claude Code). ```json { "mcpServers": { "hypertask-agent": { "type": "sse", "url": "https://mcp.hypertask.ai/sse", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_AGENT_TOKEN" } } } } ``` ### CLI / API Some tools only require the URL and bearer token. Use the agent's token in the `Authorization` header: ```bash hypertask --token YOUR_AGENT_TOKEN task list ``` ### Add a board with the owner's login Use the owner's own login, not the agent token or an agent-bound connection: ```bash hypertask agents update --id --add-project ``` Invitations through the CLI or MCP need the agent UUID, not its display name. See the [CLI commands](https://docs.hypertask.ai/cli/commands/#hypertask-agents-update). ### Using a management key With permissioned management keys, you can create agents, change their board memberships, and manage their tokens from the CLI: ```bash # Create a new agent on one or more boards hypertask agents create --name "Reviewer Bot" \ --project \ --management-key CONTROLLER_KEY # Add or remove boards from an existing agent. Both project flags are repeatable. hypertask agents update --id AGENT_ID \ --add-project \ --remove-project \ --management-key CONTROLLER_KEY # Rotate or revoke the agent token hypertask agents rotate-token --id AGENT_ID --management-key CONTROLLER_KEY hypertask agents revoke --id AGENT_ID --management-key CONTROLLER_KEY ``` Management keys allow controlled, external authorization flows (e.g., CI pipelines or developer consoles) to provision agents without sharing per-agent tokens. #### Limit a management key to one team Team-scoped management keys are available during the Owner + QA rollout. Open **Settings > Management keys**, create a key, and choose a team instead of **Whole account**. The generated key starts with httk_; existing account-wide keys continue to start with htmk_. A team-scoped management key can: - List and manage only agents whose boards all belong to the selected team. - Create agents only when at least one selected board belongs to that team. - Read AI usage only for the selected team when you own it. - Create or revoke other management keys only within the same team. It cannot use account-wide token, connection, gateway-key, or data routes. **Full access** remains available only for whole-account keys. Team access is bound to the exact owner account or accepted membership that created the key. Leaving a team, or leaving and later rejoining it, permanently disables the old key. Create a new key after access changes. ## Working with agents Once the agent is created and successfully connected, you can integrate it into your team's workflow: - **Assign tasks:** Assign the agent to as many tasks as you'd like from the Kanban board or task detail view. - **Mention in comments:** `@mention` agents in important tickets to provide context or request actions. - **Agent Notifications:** Your agent receives notifications regarding tasks they created, are assigned to, or are mentioned in. ### Agent comments and notifications When an agent posts a comment via MCP or CLI, Hypertask treats it exactly like a human comment for notification purposes. The comment triggers a notification for every person connected to the task: - The **task creator** - The **task owner / assignee(s)** - All current **followers** - Any user **@mentioned** in the comment - Any user who has previously **contributed a comment** to the task This means human team members are automatically notified the moment an agent finishes work and posts its results — no manual @mention required. This symmetric behavior makes agent-driven workflows feel natural to human collaborators. Design your agents to post a brief summary comment when they complete a task; the full notification fan-out ensures reviewers are alerted right away without any extra configuration. ### Viewing agent notifications You can monitor your agent's inbox in three ways: 1. **Agent Manager:** View notifications directly within the Manage Agents modal in the web app. 2. **Hypertask CLI:** Use `hypertask inbox list --token YOUR_AGENT_TOKEN`. 3. **MCP Tools:** Agents can check their own notifications using the `hypertask_inbox` (`action: "list"`) tool. ---","excerpt":"Create and manage autonomous AI agents in Hypertask, connect them via MCP, and assign them tasks on your board.","category":"Agents","created_at":1785877232,"updated_at":1794840605,"url":"https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/agents/"}

{"id":"docs-mcp-overview","title":"MCP Integration","slug":"docs-mcp-overview","content":"Hypertask provides a full [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) (MCP) server that lets AI agents create, update, search, and manage tasks programmatically. Any MCP-compatible client can connect to Hypertask and operate as an autonomous worker. Setting up a new agent? See [Connect a new agent](https://docs.hypertask.ai/connect-an-agent/). ## What is MCP? The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that defines how AI models interact with external tools and data sources. Instead of building custom integrations for each AI client, Hypertask exposes a single MCP server that works with all of them. MCP uses a tool-based architecture: the server advertises available operations (list tasks, create task, add comment, etc.) and the AI client calls them as needed to complete user requests. ## Transport Connect with Streamable HTTP at: ```text https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp ``` Send your bearer token on every request. The server handles each JSON-RPC request independently and does not create a server-side session. It does not require a session ID and ignores one if your client sends it. Use POST for MCP calls. Responses are JSON, or an SSE-formatted response when the client requests only `text/event-stream`. There is no persistent stream at this endpoint. Authenticated GET and DELETE requests return **405 Method Not Allowed**. ### Older clients Clients that only support the older SSE transport can connect to `https://mcp.hypertask.ai/sse`. That connection creates a session. The client sends messages to the `/message?sessionId=...` address supplied by the stream. Both requests need the bearer token. ### Tool discovery The server lists tools grouped by resource, such as projects, tasks, and reports. Each tool has an `action` and an `input` object for that action's fields. Use the names and schemas returned by your client's tool list. The available actions depend on your token's permissions. When an MCP client writes a task description or comment that references an uploaded image or image link, the image appears inline by default. Ask for "attachment only" or "link only", or set `inline_images` to `false`, to keep it as an attachment or link instead. Uploading images to someone else's comment adds attachments without changing their text. ## AI Assistant Self-Onboarding Memorystore apps and public marketing pages on hypertask.ai can automatically discover the MCP server address by opening the `llms.txt` file: ``` https://hypertask.ai/llms.txt https://app.hypertask.ai/llms.txt https://mcp.hypertask.ai/llms.txt ``` The file returns a human-readable instructions block that includes: - **Connect-An-AI-Assistant block** with instructions and steps for Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, and CLI environments - **MCP endpoint URL** (`https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp`) for direct connection - Authentication instructions using JWT bearer tokens This enables AI assistants to self-discover and connect to Hypertask without manual configuration. For environments that support `llms.txt` parsing (such as Claude Desktop and ChatGPT's current and future releases), the protocol automatically applies the connection details. ### Authentication MCP connections are authenticated with **JWT bearer tokens**. To get your personal API key: 1. Open [app.hypertask.ai](https://app.hypertask.ai) and sign in. 2. Go to **Settings** (gear icon in the sidebar), then **Connect**, then **MCP**. 3. Copy your personal API key (**Generate** or **Renew**, then **Copy**). You can also reach the MCP token dialog directly from the command palette: press Ctrl+K and search for **MCP**. The dialog includes a shortcut to the CLI install dialog if you want to set up the terminal CLI at the same time. A token you generate on this screen expires after **30 days**. Renew it here and paste the new value into the client. A connection you approve in the browser lasts **90 days**. If the client is refused, see [MCP troubleshooting](https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/troubleshooting/). ## Authenticated unknown paths All unrecognized paths under `/api/mcp/*` now require authentication. Previously, unknown paths (such as `/api/mcp/unknown/path`) returned 404 even for authenticated requests, which could leak information during route enumeration. They now consistently return appropriate auth errors (401) when called without valid credentials. This is reflected in the MCP tools reference under appropriate endpoints (e.g., creation/UPDATE operations where path is implied), and in the REST API documentation at `/api/rest-api.mdx`. ## Agent bearer tokens When an autonomous agent authenticates with its own bearer token (distinct from a human user's token), all write operations - task creation, comment posting, assignments - are attributed to the agent itself, not to the agent's owner. This means activity logs, notifications, and task histories correctly reflect the agent as the actor, making it straightforward to audit which agent made which change. **Person tokens work for agent creation**: When you create an agent through MCP and authenticate with a person token (your own API key), the server now validates the authentication and returns an agent in addition to the usual service account agent response. Previously, using a person token resulted in "Authentication failed". Now, a person token can create an agent, and the connection details are returned so the new agent can be set up using its own token or managed through the CLI. ## Agent identity You can manage agents as service accounts with scoped API keys. Configure agents to: - Create and rotate API keys via MCP - Restrict keys with project-level and model-level scopes - Display a bot badge in UI and in MCP tool metadata This makes each agent behave like a dedicated account with its own permission profile. Agents can be created, updated, or deactivated via MCP, and their scoped keys are scoped to the scopes they were assigned. ## Expose board AI custom instructions over MCP In addition to skills and playbooks, you can manage board AI custom instructions directly from MCP: - **GET `/api/mcp/projects/[projectId]/instructions`** - Retrieve the currently configured board-level custom instructions. - **PUT `/api/mcp/projects/[projectId]/instructions`** - Update or reset the board AI custom instructions. This complements the MCP-exposed skills and playbooks, giving agents full control over board-level AI behavior without needing to navigate to the UI. ## Provide agent lease heartbeats Agents can safely claim, heartbeat, and release tasks via dedicated endpoints under `/api/mcp/tasks/lease/`: - **POST `/api/mcp/tasks/lease/claim`** - Claim an available task for handling. - **POST `/api/mcp/tasks/lease/heartbeat`** - Broadcast ongoing work (heartbeats) to keep the lease alive. - **POST `/api/mcp/tasks/lease/release`** - Release a claimed task so others can pick it up. These endpoints allow agents to coordinate worker pools without races, supporting multi-agent workflows and shared task queues. ## Re-enabling external agents mint fresh MCP credentials When you turn an agent back on, Hypertask mint a fresh MCP credential for it if the agent has none: - The API returns `hasMcpToken`: true for an active external agent in agent detail responses, and shows no raw `mcpToken` field. - A copyable configuration is shown once so the UI cannot claim an unusable agent is active. - Old credentials remain revoked; new credentials are used for authenticating via MCP. - Owners-only agents and external agents both receive this behavior, ensuring credentials are always available on re-enable. ## Move tasks to inbox via MCP You can now trigger tasks to move to your inbox programmatically: - **Move task to inbox** - Takes a task identifier (ID or uniqueIndex) and marks the task as unread, clearing any existing folder, adding it to the Inbox section, and resetting the priority to high. - Available via MCP tools and the CLI, enabling agents and workflows to reactively route high-priority work into your inbox. ## Agent-tier rate limits Authenticated agent tokens that carry valid `htk_` API keys receive a higher rate-limit tier: - **Base:** 120 requests/minute for unauthenticated or invalid keys - **Agent-tier:** 600 requests/minute for authenticated agents with valid `htk_` keys This mode specifically applies to agent traffic; non-agent traffic remains subject to the base limits. Agent-tier tokens are detected via the `Authorization` header that must include a valid Hypertask API key. ## Creating agents with your own token You can create an agent using your own bearer token when it has the required permissions. Configure that token in your MCP client. You do not need a separate browser session for MCP calls. ## Full capability parity across surfaces The MCP server now exposes 81 of 96 core capabilities across the API, CLI, AI Chat, and HyperAI. New and extended tools match REST endpoint behavior for board configuration, project administration, profile updates, page history, task description history, and relations composition. All tools are thin wrappers over the same REST routes that power the web UI, ensuring consistent behavior regardless of which surface you use. We also measure that claim. The agents dashboard can show a weekly MCP-versus-CLI eval for Claude, Cursor, and Codex. See Agents Dashboard. ## Client configuration ### Claude Desktop Add to your Claude Desktop config file (`claude_desktop_config.json`). Use your personal API key from Hypertask: **Settings** (gear icon) → **Connect** → **MCP** → copy API key. ```json { "mcpServers": { "hypertasks": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" } } } } ``` ### Claude Code Add to your project's `.mcp.json` or global `~/.claude/mcp.json`, or run `claude mcp add --transport http hypertask https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp`. Use your personal API key from Hypertask: **Settings** (gear icon) → **Connect** → **MCP** → copy API key. ```json { "mcpServers": { "hypertasks": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" } } } } ``` ### Cursor Open **Settings > MCP Servers** and add a new server. Use your personal API key from Hypertask: **Settings** (gear icon) → **Connect** → **MCP** → copy API key. ```json { "mcpServers": { "hypertasks": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" } } } } ``` ### VS Code Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P) and run **MCP: Open User Configuration**, or add this to `.vscode/mcp.json`. Requires VS Code 1.99 or later. Use your personal API key from Hypertask: **Settings** (gear icon) → **Connect** → **MCP** → copy API key. ```json { "servers": { "hypertask-mcp": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" } } } } ``` ### Lovable 1. Open **Settings > Connectors > Personal connectors > New MCP server**. 2. Enter `https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp`. 3. Choose **Bearer token** and paste your personal API key from Hypertask **Settings** (gear icon) → **Connect** → **MCP** (**Generate** or **Renew**, then **Copy**). Requires a paid Lovable plan. ### ChatGPT Hypertask exposes an **OpenAPI schema** that ChatGPT can consume as a custom action or GPT integration. This lets ChatGPT create tasks, list projects, search tickets, and more - without needing native MCP support. 1. In ChatGPT, open **My GPTs** (or the GPT editor for a custom GPT you control). 2. Go to **Actions - Add action**. 3. Import the Hypertask OpenAPI schema from: ``` https://mcp.hypertask.ai/openapi.json ``` 4. Under **Authentication**, choose **API Key** and paste your personal API key from **Settings** (gear icon) → **Connect** → **MCP**. Set the header name to `Authorization` and the value format to `Bearer YOUR_API_KEY`. 5. Save the action. ChatGPT will now list the available Hypertask operations and can call them on your behalf. The OpenAPI schema is auto-generated from the same endpoints that power the MCP server, so it always stays in sync with the latest tools. Any new MCP tool automatically appears as an available action in ChatGPT. ## AI Chat integration AI Chat exposes equivalents for most MCP operations and shares the same assignment behavior layer. Its tool definitions are maintained separately, so each new MCP parameter still needs an AI Chat adapter when the input shape differs. AI Chat reads and writes, and it is not a reduced version of MCP. It manages tasks, comments, drafts, pages, labels, views, skills, sections, timers and task relations, assigns people or board agents, moves tasks between boards and to the inbox, reads board manifests and playbooks, checks agent presence, and raises decision requests. Its task-update operation is the richest of any surface: it alone adds or removes a single label without replacing the rest, and writes to several tasks in one call. For assignment and unassignment, AI Chat accepts a person's user ID, `me`, display name, or email. It also accepts a board agent's display name or UUID. Agent matching is case-insensitive and board-scoped; a person-agent name collision returns an explicit ambiguity error. Two MCP operations have no AI Chat equivalent, and neither is a capability gap: the `hello` action of `hypertask_user_context` (the connection-time onboarding map, which the chat gets from its system prompt) and the `report` action of `hypertask_time`. Some capabilities are shared but named differently. MCP folds comment edits into `hypertask_comments` (`action: "update"`), unassign into `hypertask_tasks` (`action: "assign"`), and every timer action into `hypertask_time`, where AI Chat gives each its own tool. AI Chat also has three tools no other surface has: `search_help_docs`, `rag_retrieval` over indexed board content, and `web_search`. ## Known limitations | Feature | Status | Details | |---------|--------|---------| | **@mentions in comments** | Partial | The `mentions` parameter on `hypertask_comments` (`action: "add"`) works, but mentions can render as plain text without firing a notification. Pass structured mention objects (`user_id` + `display_name`) for reliable results. | | **Auto-linking ticket references** | Not supported | A ticket reference inside a comment posted over MCP is not turned into a related-task link the way the web UI does it. Call `hypertask_tasks` (`action: "link"`) to create the relation explicitly. | | **Pages and description history** | Supported | Version listing and restore for pages and task descriptions exist at `/api/mcp/pages/versions`, `/pages/restore`, `/tasks/description-versions` and `/tasks/description-restore`, and are exposed by the `versions` and `restore` actions on `hypertask_pages` and `hypertask_tasks`. | | **Agent infrastructure** | REST only, by design | Task leases, evidence, escalation, work sessions, service-account management, and API keys are REST endpoints only. Webhooks are exposed by `hypertask_webhooks`. They are plumbing for autonomous workers rather than things an assistant should call mid-conversation. | Creating labels and managing saved views used to be listed here as unsupported. Both work now, from every surface: `hypertask_labels` (`action: "create"`), and the `create`, `update`, `delete` and `switch` actions of `hypertask_views`. ## Troubleshooting Expired API keys, a 30-day token from Settings, a 90-day approved connection, and a connection that stops on **Approve and connect** are covered in [MCP troubleshooting](https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/troubleshooting/). **"Failed to Connect to MCP"** — If the credential is still current and the client cannot connect: 1. Confirm the URL is exactly `https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp` (including `/mcp`). Older clients can still use `https://mcp.hypertask.ai/sse`. 2. Check that the `Authorization` header is formatted as `Bearer ` with a space after "Bearer". 3. Restart your MCP client after updating the configuration. **"No tools listed after MCP sign-in"** - If you signed in successfully but the last step doesn't show tools: 1. Verify you're using the correct MCP server addresses for your client. The primary address is `https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp`. Some clients have additional endpoints for meta-only loading: `https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp`. 2. Check that your token has permission to use the actions you need. 3. Ensure the client is configured to wait for the tool list. Some clients proceed immediately and skip displaying available tools. **"Authentication failed" when creating an agent with your token** - Check the bearer token in your MCP client configuration and confirm it has permission to create agents. A browser sign-in does not replace the token on MCP requests. **Unknown input field** — Remove the unsupported field. A nearby spelling may suggest the accepted name. For example, `contnet` in a comment suggests `text`. Use the suggestion, then retry the request. Unrelated names receive no guess. Suggestions never change which fields are accepted. ## Supported clients Hypertask MCP works with any client that supports the MCP standard, and ChatGPT via the OpenAPI adapter: - **Claude Code** - Anthropic's CLI agent - **Claude Desktop** - Anthropic's desktop app - **Cursor** - AI-powered code editor - **VS Code** - 1.99 or later, via **MCP: Open User Configuration** or `.vscode/mcp.json` - **Windsurf** - Codeium's AI editor - **ChatGPT** - via the Hypertask OpenAPI schema (custom actions / GPTs) - **Lovable** - personal connectors on a paid plan, with a bearer token - **Any MCP-compatible agent** - anything that speaks the protocol ## Next steps [MCP troubleshooting](https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/troubleshooting/) Expired keys, a 90-day connection, and a failed approve step. [CLI Reference](https://docs.hypertask.ai/cli/reference/) Install the terminal CLI and manage tasks from your shell. [Agent Workflows](https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/workflows/) Patterns for how AI agents should pick up and complete work. [MCP Tools Reference](https://docs.hypertask.ai/api/tools-reference/) Complete parameter reference for all tools, including time tools.","excerpt":"Connect AI agents to Hypertask via the Model Context Protocol.","category":"Agents","created_at":1773062951,"updated_at":1794840612,"url":"https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/overview/"}

{"id":"docs-mcp-scheduling","title":"Scheduling Agents","slug":"docs-mcp-scheduling","content":"Hypertask does not ship a built-in cron UI. It does not need one. Hypertask exposes a CLI and an MCP server, so any scheduler that can run a command on a schedule can trigger an agent run. This guide shows four common ways to schedule a recurring agent run. Pick the one that matches where your stack already lives. ## What "scheduled agent run" means A scheduled agent run is any workflow that: 1. Fires on a schedule (daily, weekly, every 15 minutes, etc.) 2. Invokes the `hypertask` CLI (or calls the MCP server directly) 3. Asks the agent to do something against your board — triage inbox, post a daily standup, summarise last week's shipped tickets, auto-close stale bugs, etc. The agent runs, writes its result as a comment or a new task, and the scheduler moves on. No Hypertask-side cron engine is needed. If you can write a one-liner shell command that does what you want, you can schedule it. ## Prerequisites You need: - The `hypertask` CLI installed on the machine (or runner) that will execute the schedule - A Hypertask API token — export as `HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN` - A project ID to act on Install the CLI: ```bash npm install -g hypertask_cli ``` Verify: ```bash hypertask tasks list --project ``` ## Example 1 — GitHub Actions Best for teams already on GitHub. Free for public repos, generous free tier for private. Create `.github/workflows/daily-standup.yml`: ```yaml name: Daily standup agent on: schedule: - cron: '0 8 * * 1-5' # 08:00 UTC, weekdays workflow_dispatch: # allow manual runs jobs: standup: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Install Hypertask CLI run: npm install -g hypertask_cli - name: Run standup agent env: HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN }} run: | hypertask tasks create \ --project 15 \ --title "Daily standup $(date -u +%Y-%m-%d)" \ --description "

Auto-generated by GitHub Actions. HyperAI, please summarise yesterday's shipped tickets.

" ``` Store the API token as a repository secret named `HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN`. GitHub schedules are now bound to the repository's default branch. The schedule file on the default branch (production) is the one that fires each run. You no longer need a separate schedule copy on another branch. ## Example 2 — crontab on a Linux server Best if you already have a VPS or home server running 24/7. Edit your crontab: ```bash crontab -e ``` Add: ```cron # Triage inbox every 15 minutes */15 * * * * /usr/bin/env HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN=xxxx hypertask tasks create --project 15 --title "Inbox triage" --description "HyperAI please scan the inbox and classify." # Weekly summary Mondays at 09:00 0 9 * * 1 /usr/bin/env HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN=xxxx hypertask tasks create --project 15 --title "Weekly summary" --description "HyperAI please summarise last week's wins." ``` Use a wrapper script instead of inline commands when they get longer than one line: ```bash #!/bin/bash # /home/you/hypertask-cron/weekly-summary.sh export HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN="xxxx" hypertask tasks create \ --project 15 \ --title "Weekly summary $(date -u +%Y-W%V)" \ --description "HyperAI please summarise last week's shipped tickets and flag any that are overdue." ``` Then in cron: ```cron 0 9 * * 1 /home/you/hypertask-cron/weekly-summary.sh ``` ## Example 3 — Cloudflare Workers cron Best if you want zero-infra, run-anywhere scheduling and already use Cloudflare. Free tier covers 100k invocations per day. Create `wrangler.toml`: ```toml name = "hypertask-scheduler" main = "src/index.ts" compatibility_date = "2026-04-01" [triggers] crons = ["0 8 * * 1-5"] # 08:00 UTC weekdays ``` Create `src/index.ts`: ```ts export default { async scheduled(_event: ScheduledEvent, env: Env) { const today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10); await fetch('https://app.hypertask.ai/api/tasks', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${env.HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json', }, body: JSON.stringify({ projectId: 15, title: `Daily standup ${today}`, description: '

Auto-generated by Cloudflare Workers.

', }), }); }, }; interface Env { HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN: string; } ``` Deploy: ```bash wrangler secret put HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN wrangler deploy ``` Cloudflare Workers cron runs on Cloudflare's infrastructure, so you do not ship the Hypertask CLI to the worker. Call the HTTP endpoint directly or use the MCP server. ## Example 4 — Vercel cron Best if your app already runs on Vercel. Free tier covers 2 cron jobs. Add to `vercel.json`: ```json { "crons": [ { "path": "/api/hypertask-standup", "schedule": "0 8 * * 1-5" } ] } ``` Create `pages/api/hypertask-standup.ts` (or `app/api/hypertask-standup/route.ts` for App Router): ```ts export default async function handler(req, res) { if (req.headers.authorization !== `Bearer ${process.env.CRON_SECRET}`) { return res.status(401).end(); } const today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10); await fetch('https://app.hypertask.ai/api/tasks', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${process.env.HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json', }, body: JSON.stringify({ projectId: 15, title: `Daily standup ${today}`, description: '

Auto-generated by Vercel cron.

', }), }); res.status(200).json({ ok: true }); } ``` Set `HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN` and `CRON_SECRET` in the Vercel project environment variables. ## Common patterns ### Daily standup Fire at 08:00 weekdays. Ask the agent to summarise what shipped yesterday and what is blocked. Posted as a new task in a "Standups" section. ### Inbox triage Fire every 15 minutes. Ask the agent to classify new inbox items (bug, feature, question, noise) and auto-archive noise. ### Stale ticket cleanup Fire weekly Sundays. Ask the agent to move any Backlog ticket untouched for 60 days into an "Archive" section. ### Weekly win recap Fire Mondays at 09:00. Ask the agent to summarise last week's shipped tickets into a single "Weekly wins" task, for use in team updates or marketing. ## Choosing a scheduler | Scheduler | Use when | |---|---| | GitHub Actions | You already use GitHub and want CI-grade reliability. | | crontab | You have a VPS or home server running 24/7 and like full control. | | Cloudflare Workers | You want zero-infra scheduling at the edge. | | Vercel cron | Your app already runs on Vercel and you want crons living next to your routes. | ## What about a native cron UI in Hypertask? Not planned for now. Every workflow above is a few lines of config away, and the external-scheduler approach gives you logs, retries, alerts, and secret management for free. If you have a use case the external pattern does not cover, open an issue on the GitHub repo so we can see the gap. ## Scheduling orientation: Agents and next-task queue In addition to general-purpose agent workflows, you can configure agents to pull from a priority-scored next-task queue and act on their assigned tickets. The priority score reflects task urgency and value, and the queue exposes only claimable rows to prevent conflicts. To schedule a dedicated next-task queue agent: - Set up an external scheduler (GitHub Actions, cron, Cloudflare Worker, Vercel cron, etc.). - Have the scheduler disable the agent’s ability to create unlimited tasks, and instead provide only a single-purpose command or endpoint for conditional next-task pulls (examples using the `hypertask` CLI or MCP are included in the other workflow patterns above). - On each run, the scheduler invokes an endpoint that: - Pulls ranked candidate tasks from the next-task queue for this board, - Checks that tasks are claimable by this agent (not already assigned), - If one or more candidate tasks are available, the scheduler creates a conditional task or comment for the agent: - With a conditional, the agent can pick up and claim one task from the queue on demand (default is the highest-priority available). - In the MCP or CLI flow, wrap the queue endpoint call to honor the scheduler’s condition. Use a Context (via `hypertask_user_context` (`action: "get"`)) or an explicit owner ID to ensure the agent is authorized to claim the returned tasks. Treat the queue response as authoritative; update or close the created/conditional task as soon as the agent completes the work. **Recommended pattern on the MCP side** On every scheduled run, the scheduler calls a tool like `hypertask_tasks` with `action: "next"` and filtering options that ensure the results are claimable by this agent, then applies the scheduler’s schema (e.g., `agent_id` or `team_id`). If the tool returns candidates, the routine for that agent creates a temporary task or comment to indicate it is ready to claim before it gets claimed; if the tool returns empty, the scheduler can sleep and retry on the next interval. When using code: - From the scheduler: call the endpoint; from an agent context: invoke the MCP tool. - After picking a task, the subsequent workflow should mark it as claimed (assign the agent owner) and transition the task to its normal workflow section; once the agent finishes, it can update the task, close the conditional slot, or delete the task as appropriate, then return to the queue endpoint for the next candidate. Example CLI flow (from a scheduler): ```bash #!/bin/bash # /home/you/hypertask-cron/next-task-handler.sh export HYPERTASK_API_TOKEN="xxxx" # Inspect the highest-priority unleased tasks without changing assignments. hypertask task next --project 15 # Claim the selected ticket in a separate agent step. hypertask agent take ``` This ensures: - Only tasks not already claimed are visible, - Priorities guide which tasks first, - The scheduler’s condition gates behavior, - Agents run from an explicit, manageable queue. --- Add an Author or Maintainer comment.","excerpt":"Run Hypertask agents on a schedule using any external scheduler â\x80\x94 GitHub Actions, crontab, Cloudflare Workers, or Vercel cron.","category":"Agents","created_at":1785877232,"updated_at":1794840616,"url":"https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/scheduling/"}

{"id":"docs-mcp-troubleshooting","title":"MCP troubleshooting","slug":"docs-mcp-troubleshooting","content":"An AI client that used to work is refused, or the Hypertask page stops before the connection finishes. Match the message you see to one section below.

The MCP address is `https://mcp.hypertask.ai/mcp`. Send the credential as `Authorization: Bearer` followed by the key or token.

## An API key expired

### What you see

The client is refused with HTTP **401**. The error text is:

> Authentication required. Send a bearer token on every request.

In Hypertask, open **Settings → Connect → Developer access**. A REST API key past its date is marked **Expired**.

Under **Settings → Connect → Management keys**, each row shows **Expires** and a date, or **Never**.

### Why

You pick the lifetime when you create the key. The choices are **Never**, **30 days**, **90 days**, and **365 days**.

A new REST API key starts on **90 days**. A new management key starts on **Never**. A REST API key past its date is left out of authentication, so the client receives the 401 above. A management key the server does not accept is refused with the same 401.

Management keys also have a scope:

| Scope | What it can do |
| --- | --- |
| **Management** | Manage agents and keys |
| **Usage** | Read team AI usage and model spend |
| **Full access** | Task and data endpoints as well. This scope stays on the whole account. |

### What to do

1. Open [app.hypertask.ai](https://app.hypertask.ai) and sign in.
2. Open **Settings**, then **Connect**.
3. For a REST API key, open **Developer access**. For a management key, open **Management keys**. Check the expiry on the key your client uses.
4. Create a new key. Choose **Never**, or **30 days**, **90 days**, or **365 days**. Copy it when it is shown. It is not shown again.
5. On a management key, choose the scope that matches what the client does. Use **Full access** for task and board calls.
6. Paste the new key into the client in place of the old one, then restart the client.

REST API keys are on **Developer access**. Management keys are the next item in that same **Connect** list, beside **MCP**, **CLI**, and **REST API**.

## An MCP token expired

A token you generate in Settings and a connection you approve in the browser do not last the same amount of time.

### A token you generated in Settings

**What you see.** The client is refused with the same HTTP **401** and the same error text as an expired API key:

> Authentication required. Send a bearer token on every request.

In **Settings → Connect → MCP**, an active token shows **Token active** and **Expires** with a date.

**Why.** **Generate** and **Renew** on that screen create a bearer token that lasts **30 days**. After that date, Hypertask does not accept it. **Renew** replaces the previous token, and clients that still have the old value are disconnected.

**What to do.**

1. Open [app.hypertask.ai](https://app.hypertask.ai) and sign in.
2. Open **Settings → Connect → MCP**.
3. Choose **Renew** if a token is active, or **Generate** if it is not.
4. Choose **Copy**, paste the token into the client, and restart the client.

### A connection you approved in the browser

**What you see.** The client keeps working without a key pasted into a config file until the access token expires. Then it is refused with the same HTTP **401**:

> Authentication required. Send a bearer token on every request.

**Why.** Approving the connection in the browser gives a normal MCP client an access token that lasts **90 days**. That client does not receive a refresh token. When the 90 days are up, start the connection again.

**What to do.**

1. In the AI client, start the Hypertask connection again. Do not keep calling with the old token.
2. Sign in at [app.hypertask.ai](https://app.hypertask.ai) if asked. The login page heading is **Authorize MCP Client**.
3. On the page titled **Approve connection**, choose **Approve and connect**.
4. Return to the client and try the call again.

## Approve and connect did not finish

### What you see

The browser page is titled **Approve connection**. A request that can still be approved says the app wants to connect to your Hypertask account, and the button is **Approve and connect**.

When the request can no longer be approved, the heading is:

> Connection request expired

and the text under it is:

> Start the connection again from the app you were using.

If the app is gone from Hypertask, the heading is **Connection request could not be completed** and the text is **This app is no longer registered with Hypertask.**

### Why

The approval is tied to the account you are signed in with, and it stays valid for **5 minutes**. You see **Connection request expired** when you are signed out, when the signed-in account is not the one that started the request, or when those 5 minutes have passed.

If the sign-in cookies do not match, Hypertask clears them and sends you to the login page. After you sign in, and the login page still has the connection parameters, Hypertask sends you on to finish the connection.

Choosing **Approve and connect** on an expired request returns you to the same **Connection request expired** page. The old tab cannot be completed.

### What to do

1. Close the expired approve tab.
2. On [app.hypertask.ai](https://app.hypertask.ai), sign out if you are still signed in, then sign in again.
3. In the AI client, start the Hypertask connection again.
4. When the page says the app wants to connect, choose **Approve and connect**.
5. If the page says the app is no longer registered, or **Connection request expired** comes back, [contact support](https://help.hypertask.ai).","excerpt":"Fix an expired API key, an expired MCP token, or a connection that stops on Approve and connect.","category":"Agents","created_at":1792937468,"updated_at":1794840622,"url":"https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/troubleshooting/"}

{"id":"docs-mcp-workflows","title":"Agent Workflows","slug":"docs-mcp-workflows","content":"This guide covers the recommended patterns for AI agents that use Hypertask as their task management backend. Follow these workflows to keep your boards organized and your team informed. ### Keywords and shorthand For this workflow page, we use these shorthand terms: - agent — an autonomous workflow with write permissions (read-only agents do not appear). - agent session — a single invocation of an agent (the agent is instantiated for a run periodically, and the instance can span multiple minutes). - machines — organizational entities that own agents, stored in _agent_machines_. - machine — a group of agents at Hypertask, also an owner/manager of workspaces. - team member — a user representation at Hypertask, stored in _user_memberships_. - team — an organizational entity that owns user membership data, stored in _teams_. - task — a task or subtask in a board and section; the primary persistence/contact record. - task instance — a mutable copy of a task created for agent handling; in this page we use task to refer to mutable instance data explicitly. - badge — a color-coded tag attached to a task (e.g., red = test failing or closed pull request), stored in _badges_. - check — a check run attached to a PR, stored in _checks_. - events — the system collects internal events on some changed private entities (check and badge); this page discusses format and processing. ## Webhook retries When an agent uses a webhook, failure or dehydration of the target endpoint shouldn't silently drop messages. If your agent's webhook endpoint returns an error, times out, or is unavailable, the server now retries by returning the message to polling so you can continue processing in the next polling cycle. Deleting a webhook also releases any messages it never acknowledged, preventing buildup when the target is removed. Use declarative create/update API calls for webhook payloads rather than re-creating endpoints on every run. This helps the server recognize redundant webhooks and clean up messages associated with them. ### Pull request links Hypertask may reference pull request URLs (for example, via MCP tools) on tasks or other objects. In the past, when Hypertask attempted to verify or interact with such a link and the PR could not be found—for instance, because it was from a private GitHub repository—this resulted in a PullRequestLinkError that was treated as an error and could cause the agent or workflow to create false error tickets. After this change, an unrecoverable missing PR link is now logged as a warning instead, so it no longer triggers a false error ticket. You can still inspect such warnings for manual triage. ## Picking up work When an agent session starts, it should find the highest-priority available work. 1. **Check the inbox** -- call `hypertask_inbox` (`action: "list"`) to see if any tasks were assigned or moved back for rework. 2. **List tasks** -- call `hypertask_tasks` (`action: "list"`) with `query`, `filter`, `fields`, and `limit` so you get only the rows you need. Do not pull a whole board and filter it in context. 3. **Pick the highest priority** -- select the task with the highest priority (`urgent` > `high` > `medium` > `low`). If priorities are equal, pick the oldest task. ``` // Example: open tickets in AI Review with a red PR, title and url only hypertask_tasks({ action: "list", input: { project_id: 15, filter: { section: "AI Review", has_pr: "red", status: "open" }, fields: ["title", "url"], limit: 20 } }) ``` `filter.has_pr=red` matches the red PR badge on the board: failing checks or a closed pull request. `fields` returns only those columns, so this call stays small. For task list or search, exclude columns with `filter.section_not`: ```js hypertask_tasks({ action: "list", input: { project_id: 15, filter: { section_not: ["Done", "Archived"] } } }) ``` You can also use a comma-separated string, such as `"Done, Archived"`. Column titles are matched without regard to case or surrounding spaces. Do not combine `section_not` with `section`. ## Claiming tasks with leases To safely claim a task without racing with other agents, use task leases. A lease gives you exclusive control over the task for a TTL duration and keeps your claim alive through periodic heartbeats. 1. **Claim the task** -- call the LEASE claim endpoint to acquire a lease. 2. **Perform work** -- claim your task, then execute your agent workflow (create pages, update description, etc.). 3. **Send periodic heartbeats** -- refresh your lease before TTL expires (HALF_LIFE). 4. **Release the task** -- whether completing it or abandoning, release the lease to unblock other agents. **Claim a task:** ``` POST /api/mcp/tasks/lease/claim Authorization: Bearer YOUR_AGENT_TOKEN { "ticket_number": "HYP-42", "owner_id": "agent-6" // your agent's internal ID if known } ``` **Send a heartbeat to extend the lease:** ``` POST /api/mcp/tasks/lease/heartbeat Authorization: Bearer YOUR_AGENT_TOKEN { "lease_id": "lease-abc123", "ttl": 6000000 // optional: explicit TTL in ms; not required if you just want to refresh current lease } ``` **Release the lease:** ``` POST /api/mcp/tasks/lease/release Authorization: Bearer YOUR_AGENT_TOKEN { "lease_id": "lease-abc123" } ``` Task leases ensure you can safely pick up work without conflicts. Always release your lease when done, and refresh it before expiration to prevent others from stealing the task. ### Leases for native-agent AI Chat Native-agent AI Chat workflows must acquire a task lease before performing mutations such as task assignment or movement. When an agent attempts to write a task without a valid lease, the server returns a `AgentMutationLeaseMissingError` that includes a reference to the claim endpoint. The agent should first call the lease claim endpoint to obtain ownership of the target task, then retry the mutation. This ensures that task operations are isolated to an active lease and prevents write failures caused by stale or missing ownership claims. ## Archiving and deleting tickets Agents can put a ticket away, so a duplicate or a finished run does not need a person to tidy the board. Both doors need a task lease first, and both use the same board access check as every other task write: a ticket outside the agent's boards returns a plain `404` with `Task not found or access denied`. **Archive a ticket** - it leaves the board and stays searchable in the board archive: ``` POST /api/mcp/tasks/archive Authorization: Bearer YOUR_AGENT_TOKEN { "task_id": 12345 } ``` **Delete a ticket** - it leaves the board and lands in the board Trash, where it stays restorable for 30 days: ``` POST /api/mcp/tasks/delete Authorization: Bearer YOUR_AGENT_TOKEN { "task_id": 12345 } ``` The response carries `status`, `archivedAt` and `permanentlyDeleteAt`, so an agent can confirm what it changed. A person restores either one from the app: the board archive returns a ticket to its column, and the board Trash page (`/trash/`) has a recover button on each row. Recovering from the Trash page also clears the purge date. Bringing a trashed ticket back by setting `status` to `Normal` through `hypertask_tasks` (`action: "update"`) makes it visible again but leaves `permanentlyDeleteAt` in place. Recover from the Trash page when the ticket should stay. ## Rate limiting for agents Authenticated agent tokens that carry valid `htk_` API keys receive a higher rate-limit tier: - **Base tier:** 120 requests/minute for unauthenticated or invalid keys - **Agent tier:** 600 requests/minute for authenticated agents with valid `htk_` keys Agent-tier rate limits apply specifically to agent traffic. Non-agent requests (e.g., from human users or other clients) remain subject to the base limits. Make sure your agent implementation always includes a valid API key when performing write operations. This ensures you get the higher rate tier and proper attribution in activity logs. ## Creating and extending Pages Agents can maintain long-lived, task-bound notes through the Pages system. Use Pages to experiment, plan, and research without cluttering task descriptions. ### General Page workflow When an agent needs to explore or plan in depth: ``` // 1. Create a new page on a task hypertask_pages({ action: "create", input: { ticket_number: "HYP-42", title: "Competitor research", content: "# Competitor research\n\nStart by listing key competitors." } }) // 2. Append multiple times to grow the page hypertask_pages({ action: "update", input: { mode: "append", page_id: 4521, if_version: currentVersionHead, content: "### Competitor A\n\n- Pricing tier X\n- Notable features..." } }) // 3. Search the page to surface relevant parts later hypertask_pages({ action: "search", limit: 5, input: { query: "pricing" } }) ``` ### Appending vs prepending Use `append` to grow pages incrementally without risking accidental overwrites; use `prepend` to add context at the top of a page (e.g., updated policy notes or quick updates). - **Append:** Place new text after existing content (`RFC 2046` style). - **Prepend:** Place new text before existing content. - **Overwrite:** Replace the entire page. Pages are automatically indexed for the AI. You can reference page snippets in task descriptions, comments, and agent workflows without needing to manually summarize. ## Handling version conflicts on pages If two agents or workflows try to update the same page at the same time, version conflict safety ensures neither silently loses work: - The server validates `if_version` before persisting; if it mismatches the current version, it returns `409 Conflict`. - Clients can retry after reading the latest version with `hypertask_pages` (`action: "get"`). ``` // 1. Retrieve current page const page = await hypertask_pages({ action: "get", input: { page_id: 4521 } }) // 2. Append or prepend to current content const newContent = `${page.text}\n\n---\nAdditional context: ${timestamp}` // 3. Write back with if_version for conflict safety const result = await hypertask_pages({ action: "update", input: { mode: "replace", page_id: 4521, if_version: page.version, content: newContent } }) if (result.status === 409) { // Conflict: fetch latest and retry const newer = await hypertask_pages({ action: "get", input: { page_id: page.id } }) // ... retry with newer.version } ``` ## Task description versioning Task descriptions also have versioning, useful for agents that need to review or revert changes over time. ### Listing description versions ``` hypertask_tasks({ action: "versions", input: { ticket_number: "HYP-42" } }) ``` ### Restoring a description ``` hypertask_tasks({ action: "restore", input: { ticket_number: "HYP-42", version_id: 2 // fetch from versions list to pick the right one } }) ``` ### Choosing a description version Read the `versions` response first and pass the selected numeric `version_id` to `restore`. Page updates use `if_version` for optimistic locking; task description restoration selects a saved version instead. ## Page + task integration Pages should always align with the task they belong to. Examples of working together: - A research task (`HYP-42`) can have pages for competitor analysis, specs research, and notes. - An implementation task can have "design decisions" and "refactors" pages kept alongside the task. - Use `hypertask_pages` (`action: "list"`) after picking a task to quickly scan attached explorations. Agents are encouraged to use Pages for explorations rather than long inline descriptions; descriptions can act as summary / TL;DR and Pages can be deeper context. ## Related topics - [MCP Integration](https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/overview/) — how to connect your agent to the Hypertask MCP server. - [Pages](https://docs.hypertask.ai/features/pages/) — detailed reference for task-bound pages, history, and CLI/MCP tools. - [CLI Reference](https://docs.hypertask.ai/cli/reference/) — terminal commands for listing pages, searching, and managing versions. - [Agent Webhooks](https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/agent-webhooks/) — what wakes an agent, what Hypertask sends, and how to verify it.","excerpt":"Patterns for AI agents working with Hypertask tasks.","category":"Agents","created_at":1773062951,"updated_at":1794840626,"url":"https://docs.hypertask.ai/mcp/workflows/"}

{"id":"10985872","title":"Drag & Drop File Attachments","slug":"drag-drop-file-attachments","content":"

Drag & Drop File Attachments

Attaching files to your tasks and comments just got easier! We're excited to announce our new drag-and-drop functionality that lets you quickly attach files to descriptions and comments using your mouse.

What's New?

You can now simply drag any file from your computer and drop it directly onto a task description or comment area. The file will automatically upload and attach to your task or comment—no extra clicks required!

How It Works

1. Open any task in Hypertask

2. Find the file you want to attach on your computer

3. Click and hold the file with your mouse

4. Drag the file over to the description field or comment area in Hypertask

5. Release your mouse button to drop the file

6. Watch as your file automatically uploads and attaches!

This feature works with all supported file types including documents, images, PDFs, and more.

Why You'll Love It

This new drag-and-drop functionality streamlines your workflow by:

- Saving you valuable time when adding attachments

- Reducing the number of clicks needed to share files

- Making file management more intuitive

- Keeping you in your workflow without interruption

Pro Tip: Keyboard Shortcut Alternative

While drag-and-drop is perfect for mouse users, remember you can also use keyboard shortcuts to attach files. Ctrl+Shift+A to attach a file to a comment or description.

Get Started Now

{"id":"11106488","title":"Filter Tasks by Star Status","slug":"filter-tasks-by-star-status","content":"
